High-End Student Housing Sector Faces Financial Strain Amid Rising Costs and Falling International Demand

30 Oct 2026, 02:31 PM IST · GlobeWire Daily Education Desk · Source: www.theguardian.com

Market Pressures Hit Luxury Student Accommodation

A combination of rising borrowing costs, a squeeze on living expenses, and shifting patterns in international student enrollment has triggered financial distress among providers of high-end purpose-built student accommodation (PBSA) across the UK. Once marketed as the ultimate modern university living experience featuring gyms, cinemas, and rooftop terraces, several private tower blocks have recently gone bust or found themselves sitting half-empty.

The downturn has left some students scrambling for alternative housing at the start of the academic year. Nathalie Sriwiboonrattan, a fourth-year game design student at Abertay University, discovered while visiting family in Thailand over the summer that the owner of her Dundee studio flat had abruptly collapsed into administration, forcing her to rapidly secure new lodging and pay moving costs for her belongings.

Affordability Gap and Falling Demand

Industry analysts point to a widening mismatch between soaring private rents and stagnant maintenance loans for domestic students. While the national average rent for PBSAs outside London stands at £191 a week including bills, top-tier en suite rooms in cities like Manchester range from £170 to £320 weekly, and London rooms command between £250 and £650.

Experts note that while demand remains resilient in major hubs like London and around Russell Group institutions, cities such as Coventry, Leeds, Nottingham, and Glasgow are experiencing oversupply. Data from the student housing charity Unipol shows that demand in Nottingham fell from a pandemic peak of 46,295 beds in 2022-23 to 42,290 beds in 2025-26, even as thousands of new PBSA beds entered the market.

Furthermore, changes in international demographics have altered the market. Martin Blakey, a former chief executive of Unipol, noted that student arrivals from China have stagnated, while incoming students from growth markets like India, Pakistan, and Nigeria tend to be more cost-conscious.

Sector Response and Broader Impacts

Major developers are actively restructuring portfolios to mitigate losses. Unite Group, the UK’s largest developer and manager of student accommodation, has moved to slim down its portfolio to focus on cities with the strongest university demand, while smaller operators face an estimated average occupancy level of 85%.

To offset vacancies, some property owners are exploring alternative models, including renting floors to young professionals or utilizing partially filled blocks for short-term hotel stays. Meanwhile, student unions and advocacy groups have raised alarms regarding broader housing accessibility, with representatives pointing out that affordability strains are driving some students toward commuting, food banks, or precarious living situations.

Official guidance from government emphasizes that higher education providers are expected to evaluate the supply and affordability of student accommodation over multi-year horizons in coordination with local planning authorities.

Practical Implications and Verification

What is Confirmed

  • Several PBSA operators and properties, such as Marketgait Apartments in Dundee, have experienced financial collapses or difficulties.
  • Occupancy rates vary significantly by region, with regional centers experiencing oversupply while prime locations maintain stronger demand.
  • A significant affordability gap exists between private PBSA rents and standard British student maintenance loans.

What Remains Unknown

  • The long-term financial viability of smaller independent PBSA developments outside Russell Group cities.
  • The exact scope of how many additional properties may pivot toward young professionals or short-term holiday lets.

How to Verify

Readers can review comprehensive market analyses and sector reports published by property agencies such as Knight Frank, data platforms like StuRents, and housing sector experts via Unipol. Official statements and policy expectations are detailed in announcements from the UK government and higher education regulators. For further details, consult the original report on [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/education/2026/oct/05/collapse-providers-high-end-student-accommodation).
